title: A Mother’s Bereavement
intro: Badawi al-Jabal dedicated this elegy to his friend Kamel Mrowa, the founder of the Beirut newspaper al-Hayat, who was shot in his office in 1966. It opens with a man watching those he loves disappear, then turns to the mother whose eyes search the line of visitors for her son. In the full poem Badawi names his own dead son Adnan among those his friend has joined. The elegy takes in Jerusalem and Sinai before it closes on the loss of a single man’s tomorrow.

translation: Why does death draw away when I call her?
Some of what I feel is bitterer than any death.
1.sharh: Death behaves like someone who can hear a summons and chooses to walk away. Even a portion of the grief he already bears would outweigh what others dread.

translation: Thirsty, I watch death’s watering place close by.
My loved ones go down to drink. I do not.
2.sharh: The paradox lies in who reaches the water. The man who thirsts for death has to watch the people he loves take their turn there.

translation: I tried to soothe my griefs with patience. What sorrow,
seeking relief from the breath of embers in embers.
3.sharh: Patience is usually the remedy offered to mourners. For him enduring the pain burns just as fiercely as giving way to it.

translation: I called my two companions, tears and fortitude.
Tears came to my aid, but fortitude failed me.
4.sharh: Tears and self-command are intimate friends he expects to answer. Only the one that lets him show his grief keeps faith.

translation: I am unarmed in the thick of battle.
Neither sword nor mail keeps harm from me.
5.sharh: To grieve is to stand in a battle with nothing in hand and no armour on the body. Every place from which he could have warded off a blow has been exposed.

translation: With one hand I fend blades off my heart.
One wipes tears from my bleeding wounds.
6.sharh: The two hands are simultaneously occupied. His wounds seem able to weep, so that blood and tears can be wiped away in a single movement.

translation: A man of genius is a stranger at home,
turning wherever hatred and envy turn.
7.sharh: He broadens the lament to the kind of loneliness a gifted person can suffer in his own country. Hatred and envy keep him company wherever he goes.

translation: And many who carry sacred messages
stand alone, singled out by their generous struggle.
8.sharh: What sets these bearers of a cause apart also leaves them lonely. Their struggle is called generous, a quality usually applied to a person’s dealings with others.

translation: Scattered by the driving wind, they have no homeland
or town to gather up their scattered grief.
9.sharh: Their dispersion has a physical force behind it, like a wind blowing things apart. No place gathers either the people or the separate pieces of their affliction.

translation: On the soil of truth’s battlefields lie
shreds of their bodies and splinters of their spears.
10.sharh: The claim that these people fought for truth leaves something visible on the ground. Their spears have undergone the same breaking as their bodies.

translation: Many who complain that the age is corrupt wrong it.
The age stayed sound. Its people went bad.
11.sharh: Calling a whole age corrupt makes time itself the accused. He gives the charge a human subject that can answer for it.

translation: You worked magic, except it was words.
You poured out opinions, except it was honey.
12.sharh: Mrowa’s writing can be named in two ways at once. What the reader receives is a reasoned opinion, while its effect on the senses is closer to a draught of honey.

translation: Critic, your love dictated your rarest lines.
Even in criticism you overflowed with tenderness.
13.sharh: Love is the voice dictating to the critic. The verb for showing tenderness also suggests being wet with dew, an image taken up at the graveside.

translation: The grave will want for neither water nor fragrance.
My eyelids are wet, and I have a heart.
14.sharh: Visiting a grave can mean bringing water or perfume. He carries both gifts within him, in the moisture of his eyes and his inward affection.

translation: I bend to kiss your blood, shed without redress.
What the veins have given is sweeter than roses.
15.sharh: Rose and veins are written with the same three consonants. Different vowels turn the familiar fragrant offering into the blood of the murdered man.

translation: Your heart’s blood, every drop that flowed,
a burning star wished for its radiance.
16.sharh: A star already burns and still envies the light of a single drop. The image makes the value of the life lost visible at a vast distance.

translation: I kept vigil amid calamity. It tore me apart
to see them asleep, untouched by sleeplessness.
17.sharh: He witnessed other people sleeping through the very calamity that kept him awake. The Arabic for witnessing and for losing sleep nearly chime.

translation: In my wasting sickness and my grief they drew close,
joining forces to set time against me.
18.sharh: Their approach might have promised help. What brings them together is the chance to urge time itself to injure a man already laid low.

translation: Mother, the pain in your tears makes
the loftiest mountains weep and the heavens quake.
19.sharh: The address is to the bereaved mother. The highest and seemingly least movable parts of the world respond bodily to what her tears contain.

translation: Mother, I have no soul left to pour
over your grief, no tears, no heart.
20.sharh: He would pour his very life over her sorrow as others pour water. Everything he might draw on in order to comfort her has been spent.

translation: Your eyes go round the visitors, asking
for the loved one who left, looking for him.
21.sharh: A funeral fills the room with visitors and leaves out the one visitor she wants. Her eyes go on asking a question those present cannot answer.

translation: Our loved ones have found joy in God’s gardens.
We suffer for them, but they are happy.
22.sharh: He speaks of the dead in the plural. In the full poem his friend and his own son Adnan are together among those whose happiness he hopes for.

translation: I visit the grave, cherish it and kiss it.
Around me stand two mockers, the unseen and eternity.
23.sharh: The grave offers a surface he can actually touch. The forces standing round it have no bodies and give him no knowledge of what lies beyond.

translation: Whenever my loved ones’ images cloud over,
I call, “Stay close to me,” though they are gone.
24.sharh: Even the images he can summon are unstable. The command reaches out at the precise moment when memory itself begins to lose its hold.

translation: By God’s light, the martyr’s spirit has never dimmed.
Wait a little. You will see the oppressors burn out.
25.sharh: The same verb means both dying down like a fire and becoming still. The murderers appear powerful for a moment, whereas the murdered man keeps his light.

translation: A war on unbelief and tyranny is kindled
by thought founded on a shining proof.
26.sharh: This is a description of a writer at work. The thing that can start a war here is an argument made persuasive by evidence.

translation: They struck you treacherously. Had they faced you,
the angry lion would have torn the hunters apart.
27.sharh: The circumstances of the killing supply the real ending. The lion and the hunters enact the alternative ending his friend deserved.

translation: Your only weapons were light and Islam.
From both came help and reinforcements at victory.
28.sharh: His friend’s resources are intellectual and religious. The reinforcements in the second half arrive from precisely the two sources named in the first.

translation: An enduring message from the father of al-Zahra
is your conquering, victorious host and all its equipment.
29.sharh: The father of al-Zahra is Muhammad. The message he brought can supply a solitary man with both the soldiers and the equipment of a victorious host.

translation: When at last their broken ranks fled in all directions
and the pride and head-high bearing of truth humbled cowardice,
30.sharh: This sentence waits for the next verse to name the figure who appears. Meanwhile a whole rout is visible in two postures, one pressed down and one held proudly upright.

translation: you came into view, your blood a sun whose glare
a man with sore eyes tries to hide behind his palm.
31.sharh: The hand is large enough to shade one damaged eye. Against a whole sun it measures the futility of the attempt to hide the bloodshed.

translation: Do not let the oppressors’ pride deceive you, even if
their towers and pillars boast against the heavens.
32.sharh: Architectural height gives power the appearance of permanence. By making the structures themselves swagger, he shows whose vanity they express.

translation: The proud ones of my people have ways perfumed
by the richness of truth. They neither exaggerate nor deny.
33.sharh: These are the qualities he wants to claim for his people. Truthfulness has both limits, saying too much and withholding what one knows, and the generous space between them.

translation: Generous ways, once strangers to bluster and resentment.
How bluster and resentment have disfigured them.
34.sharh: The very words for what those people once escaped return as the forces that deform their conduct. The protest now includes his own community.

translation: They disowned ancient glory, though it is morning light.
It hurts the eyes. Sore eyes cannot hurt the light.
35.sharh: Morning light can sting a diseased eye. The poet reverses the terms to show how little an eye’s complaint can do to the sun.

translation: Let those content with an undefended peace be ransoms
for those who met calamity head-on and rose to face it.
36.sharh: The language of ransom fixes the value of each group. Those who enjoy the peace owe their security to those willing to keep it.

translation: Jerusalem is a battle. Its field is crowded
with armoured fighters and the onrushing horses of truth.
37.sharh: He can now see a whole battlefield in the name of one city. The streaming horses belong to a cause that the poet personifies.

translation: Sinai’s sand is a grave that rises, shaking,
with all who fell by treachery and were never buried.
38.sharh: The dead have no individual graves. Calling the entire sandy expanse their grave lets it rise and testify on their behalf.

translation: A thousand echoes cry out in the sand, waiting
for a brave rider to rouse the deserts.
39.sharh: An echo multiplies a call without answering it. The rider is the human reply that all this sound is waiting for.

translation: I see the abject, while battle mocks them.
They made threats of war. All they did was promise.
40.sharh: Two closely related verbs pull the boast apart. The first makes a menacing threat, the second leaves only a promise of something yet to happen.

translation: When the crash of thunder terrified everyone who heard it
and night’s lightning troubled the onlookers’ dreams,
41.sharh: Sound reaches the hearers and light reaches the beholders, then follows them into their dreams. The result of the upheaval has still to appear.

translation: the dust cleared to show a tyrant’s broken body,
and the lion walked proudly through his own forests.
42.sharh: At last the eye can distinguish two figures. The tyrant is in pieces on the ground and the creature free to move again is the lion.

translation: The highest heaven greeted another sphere
with stars, hours before dawn, and breaking day.
43.sharh: His friend’s qualities have grown into a sky of their own. The real heavens can look across and greet it as another realm of light.

translation: This sky is a book of scattered visions.
Every star in it is a thought and a belief.
44.sharh: He changes the way the heavens can be approached, from a space to look at into a text to read. A star can now carry the content of a mind.

translation: I have a world that fills this world and is filled by it,
and a world apart, fragrant with secrets.
45.sharh: One of his worlds exchanges everything with the common world. The other is private, perceptible in the poem chiefly through the scent he gives it.

translation: My spirit springs forward to follow you in death.
Harsh fate gives its ruling, and it slows.
46.sharh: The impulse to follow the dead returns from the opening. An outside power changes even the speed at which his spirit can move.

translation: Life after you is empty talk, with neither delight
nor happy hope, nor even grief.
47.sharh: The list ends by removing even sorrow. What is left of life scarcely makes more sense to him than idle talk.

translation: How wretched the man whose hopes turned back
to yesterday, whose today closed and whose tomorrow died.
48.sharh: Hope ordinarily looks forward. Its turning back to yesterday leaves the present folded away and gives death, once summoned by the speaker, a final victim in tomorrow.

1.1.2.head: المَنِيَّة
1.1.2.meaning: Death, here addressed as someone able to turn away.

2.1.3.head: وِرد
2.1.3.meaning: Going to water to drink, also the watering place itself.

2.1.5-6.head: عَن كَثَب
2.1.5-6.meaning: “At close quarters”, from a short distance away.

3.1.1.head: عَلَّلَ
3.1.1.meaning: Tried to soothe or give temporary consolation.

3.2.5.head: اِبتَرَدَ
3.2.5.meaning: Sought something to cool himself with.

4.1.2.head: خِدن
4.1.2.meaning: An intimate companion. The verse calls on two.

4.1.6.head: جَلَد
4.1.6.meaning: Fortitude, the strength to bear hardship.

5.2.7.head: الزَّرَد
5.2.7.meaning: Linked metal rings, hence a coat of mail.

6.1.5.head: مُهجَة
6.1.5.meaning: The heart’s blood, then life itself.

8.1.3.head: مُقَدَّسَة
8.1.3.meaning: Sacred or consecrated. The adjective takes the accusative of the object “messages”. The reciter gives it the genitive ending also shown on the video card.

9.2.2.head: أَشتات
9.2.2.meaning: Scattered parts that have ceased to form a whole.

10.2.4.head: مُرّان
10.2.4.meaning: Wood used for spear shafts, hence the spears themselves.

10.2.5.head: قِصَد
10.2.5.meaning: Splinters or lengths of broken spear shafts.

12.1.6.head: كَلِم
12.1.6.meaning: Words or utterances, here a journalist’s writing.

12.2.5.head: شَهَد
12.2.5.meaning: Honey, especially honey in the comb.

13.1.5.head: فَريدَة
13.1.5.meaning: A choice pearl, hence a particularly fine expression.

14.2.5.head: كَبِد
14.2.5.meaning: Literally the liver, conceived as the seat of deep feeling.

15.2.7.head: الوُرُد
15.2.7.meaning: Veins, a plural of warid identified in the diwan’s own note.

19.2.1-2.head: شُمُّ البَواذِخ
19.2.1-2.meaning: “The highest of the towering ones”, the great summits of mountains.

20.1.6.head: أَغدَقَ
20.1.6.meaning: Poured out abundantly, originally said of water.

23.1.1.head: أَلَمَّ
23.1.1.meaning: Stopped at a place for a visit.

23.1.3.head: أَغلى
23.1.3.meaning: Held it dear, cherished it. The diwan and the verse card give ughlihi. The consonant is faint in the recording and the word can also be heard as ulihi.

25.1.3.head: نور
25.1.3.meaning: By the light of God. The diwan has ka-nur, “like the light”.

25.2.1.head: لَبِّث
25.2.1.meaning: Wait a little, give it time.

26.2.4.head: الزَّهراء
26.2.4.meaning: Bright or radiant, here said of a demonstrably clear case.

27.2.3-4.head: الضَّيغَمُ الحَرِد
27.2.3-4.meaning: “The angry lion”, the imagined prey that turns on its hunters.

29.1.3-4.head: أَبو الزَّهراء
29.1.3-4.meaning: Abu al-Zahra, “father of al-Zahra”, Muhammad as the father of Fatima.

29.2.1.head: عَديد
29.2.1.meaning: The numerical strength of a body of supporters or troops.

29.2.4.head: عُدَّة
29.2.4.meaning: Equipment or arms provided for a campaign, distinguished here from the fighting strength of the men.

30.1.5.head: فُلول
30.1.5.meaning: The scattered remnants of a defeated force.

30.2.5.head: الصَّيَد
30.2.5.meaning: A proud carriage of the head, originally a tilt of the neck.

31.2.4.head: الرَّمِد
31.2.4.meaning: Someone with inflamed eyes, for whom strong light is painful.

33.1.2.head: الصّيد
33.1.2.meaning: Proud, high-spirited people, literally those who hold their heads high.

36.2.3.head: زاحَمَ
36.2.3.meaning: Pressed against or grappled with. The diwan uses the shorter verb zahamu.

36.2.6.head: نَهَدَ
36.2.6.meaning: Rose to an occasion, advanced to meet it.

37.2.2.head: الكُماة
37.2.2.meaning: Warriors fully covered by their arms and armour.

38.1.2.head: سَيناء
38.1.2.meaning: Sinai, the Egyptian peninsula between the gulfs of Suez and Aqaba.

38.1.3.head: لَحد
38.1.3.meaning: A recess in a grave for the body, hence the grave itself.

39.2.5.head: نَجِد
39.2.5.meaning: Brave and ready to face danger.

40.2.2.head: الوَغى
40.2.2.meaning: The din of fighting, hence battle itself.

42.1.2.head: النَّقع
42.1.2.meaning: Dust raised into a cloud, especially in battle.

42.2.2.head: خَطَرَ
42.2.2.meaning: Walked with a proud, swinging gait.

43.2.4.head: الرَّأَد
43.2.4.meaning: The first part of the day as the light grows.

47.2.4.head: هانٍ
47.2.4.meaning: Pleasant or happy, a shortened form of hani'.

47.2.6.head: كَمَد
47.2.6.meaning: Grief that stays bottled up inside.
